question: One of the demands made at the recent farmers’ protests in a number of EU Member States is an end to unfair competition from producers in third countries that have less strict laws on the regulation and use of plant protection products, as some of these products are prohibited in the EU. In view of this: 1.
What measures is the Commission considering to meet the farmers’ demands?

Has it considered revising Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 concerning the placing of plant protection products on the market to simplify the procedure to approve plant protection products currently banned in the EU and could the EFSA study indicate that they are not harmful so that they can be used in the same way as they are used by farmers in third countries?

Similarly, with a view to preventing unfair competition, will it propose a reform to ensure better border controls of imports from third countries containing plant protection substances that are banned in the EU so as to ensure that they comply with the existing MRLs and tighten them up where necessary?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2024) Food products placed on the EU market, regardless of their origin, must comply with the food safety criteria laid down in EU legislation. Member States monitor compliance with Maximum Residues Levels (MRLs)1 of pesticides based on an EU-coordinated multi-annual control programme2 and risk-based national control programmes3.
For active substances not approved in the EU because of concerns for consumer health, MRLs are set at the limit of determination (technical zero).

Where a risk of contamination of products imported from a third country is identified, including in particular for active substances prohibited in the EU to comply with the protection goals of Regulation (EC) No 1107/20094, the Commission may take measures by amending Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17935 requiring reinforced import checks at border control posts at harmonised frequencies and certification by the exporting country.

By regularly introducing amendments to the Annexes of that Regulation, the Commission ensures that controls on commodities imported from third countries remain risk-based, in order to safeguard the health of the consumers in the EU.

Applicants may at any time submit an application for approval of an active substance to be used in plant protection products – this applies also to active substances no longer approved in the EU which might be used with new technologies demonstrating that the strict levels of protection of human health and the environment provided under Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 are complied with.

Under this Regulation the burden of proof to demonstrate a safe use lies on the applicant and not on the authorities; the uses authorised in third countries could also be proposed for approval in the EU.
1 Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 February 2005 on
maximum residue levels of pesticides in or on food and feed of plant and animal origin and amending Council Directive 91/414/EEC, OJ L 70, 16.3.2005. 2 https://food.ec.europa.
